title: Windows Support 1: Desktop & Access Essentials
subject: File Permissions & Client Management
description: Step into the shoes of a Tier 1 Support Tech. You'll solve everyday tickets involving NTFS permissions, Group Policy, file system limitations, and domain connectivity using an evidence-first workflow.
reportOverview: This report evaluates your ability to troubleshoot user-facing issues. Key skills tested: NTFS vs Share permissions, Active Directory group membership, and file system architecture.
evidenceInstructions:
Instructions:
1) Read the user's complaint and examine the artifacts.
2) Use the initial step to gather evidence (Effective Access, ipconfig, or Disk Management).
3) Diagnose the logic error (Deny vs Allow, FAT32 vs NTFS).
4) Apply the Fix and review the Resolution Insight to master the concept.

tickets.title: HR New Hire Access Request
tickets.summary: A new employee in HR, Sarah Jenkins, reports she cannot open the 'HR_Private' folder on the shared drive. Other HR staff have no issues.
artifact: Error: 'Windows cannot access \\FileServer\HR_Private - Access is Denied'
AD Check: User is a member of 'Domain Users' and 'HR_Department' groups.
Folder Security: 'HR_Staff' group has Modify permissions; 'HR_Department' is not listed.

triage.q: What is the most efficient way to see exactly why Sarah is being blocked?
options: Ask Sarah to restart her computer three times
Check the 'Effective Access' tab in the folder's Advanced Security settings for sjenkins
Delete the HR folder and recreate it
Give Sarah the Domain Admin password temporarily

diagnosis.q: Sarah is in 'HR_Department' but the folder gives access to 'HR_Staff'. What is the issue?
options: The user is not a member of the specific security group that has NTFS permissions for that folder
The folder is encrypted with BitLocker
The server is out of licenses

fix.q: How do you resolve this according to standard onboarding procedures?
options: Add Sarah's individual user account directly to the folder's security tab
Add Sarah to the 'HR_Staff' security group in Active Directory
Disable NTFS permissions on the File Server

debrief.summary: Direct permissions are harder to manage than group-based ones.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: In enterprise environments, access is managed via the AGDLP principle (Accounts into Global groups, into Domain Local groups, which are assigned Permissions). Assigning permissions to a group rather than an individual ensures that as staff change, you only manage AD membership rather than editing thousands of folder ACLs.

tickets.title: USB Storage Capacity Error
tickets.summary: A user is trying to copy a 5GB database export to a 16GB USB drive. The drive is empty, but Windows returns an error saying 'The file is too large for the destination file system.'

triage.q: The drive has enough space, but the file won't copy. What property should you look at first in Disk Management?
options: The drive letter assigned to the USB
The File System type (FAT32, NTFS, or exFAT)
The brand of the USB drive
The color of the USB port (2.0 vs 3.0)

diagnosis.q: Why does a 5GB file fail to copy to a 16GB FAT32 volume?
options: FAT32 has a maximum individual file size limit of 4GB
Windows 10 does not support USB drives larger than 4GB
The file is infected with a virus

fix.q: How do you enable the user to carry this 5GB file?
options: Compress the file into five 1GB parts
Reformat the USB drive as NTFS or exFAT
Update the USB drivers in Device Manager

debrief.summary: File systems have architectural limits regardless of storage size.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: The File Allocation Table (FAT32) uses a 32-bit value to track file sizes, creating a hard limit of 4GB (minus 1 byte) per file. To handle modern data sizes, NTFS or exFAT must be used, as they support significantly larger files (up to 16 Exabytes for NTFS).

tickets.title: Workstation Trust Relationship Failure
tickets.summary: A user returning from a 3-month leave tries to log in. They receive: 'The trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed.'
artifact: Network: Connectivity to DC is confirmed.

triage.q: What tool can you use to verify the secure channel status?

diagnosis.q: What happened to this computer's account?
options: The machine account password (managed by netlogon) is out of sync with the domain

fix.q: What is the best way to fix the trust?

debrief.summary: Computer accounts have passwords just like users do.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Windows computers change their 'machine password' in Active Directory every 30 days by default. If a PC is off for months, it may miss multiple updates, causing the 'Secure Channel' to break. Rejoining the domain creates a new Security Identifier (SID) and resets this trust.

tickets.title: Folder Inheritance Discrepancy
tickets.summary: A manager created a sub-folder. Even though the team has access to the parent folder, no one can see the new sub-folder.
artifact: Security: Only the Manager is listed on the sub-folder ACL.

triage.q: In the Security tab, how can you tell if a permission is inherited?
options: Inherited permissions have a grey checkbox
They are listed at the bottom
Inheritance was disabled, so the sub-folder didn't receive the 'Allow' entries from the parent
The team is in the wrong OU

fix.q: How do you restore team access?

debrief.summary: Inheritance is the flow of permissions from top to bottom.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: By default, sub-folders 'inherit' permissions from their parent. Disabling inheritance (breaking the link) prevents this flow. Re-enabling it ensures consistency across the file structure and reduces the risk of 'permission drift' where sub-folders have different security than their parents.

tickets.title: Duplicate Computer Object Block
tickets.summary: You are joining a laptop named 'LAPTOP-05' to the domain. You get 'The account already exists' and access is denied.
artifact: Search: 'LAPTOP-05' exists in AD, created 2 years ago.
Status: The old device was decommissioned but never removed from AD.

triage.q: Where do you check for existing computer names in AD?

options: AD won't allow a new device to hijack an existing computer account's SID without permission
Delete or Reset the old object in AD before joining

debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Every computer in AD has a unique Security Identifier (SID). If you try to join a new machine with an existing name, AD sees it as a security risk (identity theft). You must 'Reset' the account to allow a new SID to be associated with that name.

tickets.title: Group Conflict: The Deny Rule
tickets.summary: James is in 'Contractors' (Deny Finance) and 'Project-A' (Allow Finance). He is blocked from the Finance folder.

options: An explicit Deny overrides any Allow, regardless of group membership

fix.q: How do you give James access?
options: Remove the 'Deny' and simply leave the 'Allow' boxes unchecked for contractors
Move him to a new OU

debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Windows uses a specific order for evaluating ACLs. An explicit 'Deny' is checked before any 'Allow'. Best practice is to avoid 'Deny' whenever possible; instead, simply 'don't grant' access. This allows users to gain access through other group memberships without being blocked.

tickets.title: Unallocated Space Management
tickets.summary: A user needs a D: drive for data, but the 1TB disk only shows a C: drive.

diagnosis.q: What must happen before a D: drive can be created?
options: The C: drive must be shrunk to create unallocated space
Shrink C: volume -> New Simple Volume on Unallocated Space

debrief.summary: Volumes are logical divisions of physical disks.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: A 'Volume' must sit within a 'Partition'. By shrinking an existing volume, you return space to an 'Unallocated' state. From there, you can create a new partition table entry and format it with a file system to create a separate drive letter (D:).

tickets.title: Share vs NTFS Constraints
tickets.summary: User has 'Full Control' on a network share but gets 'Access Denied' when saving. NTFS is set to 'Read'.

triage.q: When combining Share and NTFS, which wins?

options: The NTFS 'Read' limit is more restrictive than the Share 'Full Control'

debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Think of Share permissions as the gate to the property and NTFS as the lock on the front door. A user must pass through BOTH. Windows evaluates both and applies the 'Most Restrictive' result. Modern admins usually set Share to 'Full Control' and manage security entirely via NTFS.

tickets.title: The Invisible Internal Drive
tickets.summary: A user installed a second SSD, but it doesn't appear in 'This PC'.
artifact: Disk Management: Disk 1 shows as 'Not Initialized' and 'Unallocated'.

triage.q: What is the state of a brand-new, unformatted disk?

options: A disk must be initialized (GPT/MBR) and a volume created before Windows assigns it a drive letter
Initialize disk -> Create New Simple Volume -> Format NTFS
Assign a letter to the C: drive

debrief.summary: Hardware needs a logical structure to be usable.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Initialization creates the partition style (GPT is the modern standard). Without a partition table and a formatted file system (NTFS), Windows cannot map the storage sectors to a drive letter that the user can interact with in File Explorer.

tickets.title: Authentication Block: Kerberos Time Skew
tickets.summary: User cannot log in. Error: 'There is a time difference between the client and the server.'

triage.q: What is the default Kerberos time skew limit?

diagnosis.q: Why does time matter for login?
options: Windows uses time for its screensaver
Kerberos tickets are timestamped to prevent replay attacks; large differences cause rejection
The server is in a different time zone

debrief.summary: Time is a critical security component in Active Directory.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Kerberos is the default auth protocol in AD. It uses 'Timestamps' to ensure that a captured login packet cannot be reused later (a Replay Attack). If the client and DC disagree by more than 5 minutes, the security handshake is aborted to protect the network.
